[00:00] Priya: Hi everyone, um, thanks for having me. I'm Priya Nair, founder and CEO of Mise AI. So, uh, I spent six years running kitchens before I ever wrote a line of code, and I want to start with a number that honestly kept me up at night when I was a sous chef. The USDA estimates that somewhere between thirty and forty percent of the US food supply is wasted. And restaurants, you know, are a huge chunk of that. In my last kitchen we were throwing out about eleven hundred dollars of product every single week, and nobody could tell me exactly why.
[00:38] Priya: So, um, the problem. Independent restaurants run on margins of like three to five percent. Food cost is their single biggest controllable expense, usually around thirty percent of revenue. But the way most kitchens track inventory is, honestly, a clipboard and a walk-in cooler at eleven p.m. on a Sunday. Counts are wrong, ordering is based on gut feel, and by the time the owner sees the P and L, the money's already, like, in the dumpster. Literally.
[01:15] Priya: Mise AI fixes that. We put a cheap camera and a shelf-weight sensor kit in the walk-in and the dry storage, and we connect to the point-of-sale. Um, every time a dish is sold, we know what should have left the shelf. Every time the door opens, we know what actually left the shelf. And the gap between those two numbers, that's waste, theft, over-portioning, or spoilage. We show it to the chef in plain English every morning, like, "you over-portioned salmon by eighteen percent yesterday, that's two hundred and twelve dollars."
[01:58] Priya: And then, uh, the part that I think is really the magic: we auto-generate the next purchase order. The chef just taps approve. We forecast demand using their sales history, the weather, local events, even, you know, whether there's a home game that night. Our customers cut food waste by an average of twenty-six percent in the first ninety days. That's not a projection, that's measured across our live kitchens.

Right side is the morning briefing, three bullet points, that's it. Chefs don't read dashboards. They read three bullet points on their phone while they're, like, drinking coffee at six a.m.

And the legacy inventory tools like MarketMan or MarginEdge are basically, you know, spreadsheets with a login. None of them actually see what's physically on the shelf.
